newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel gets mixed views on air quality plan.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel gets mixed views on air quality plan.

text.p: In the first congressional hearing on the Clinton administration's controversial call for stricter air standards, a Senate panel Wednesday got mixed views from scientists on whether the proposal had adequate scientific backing.
The chairman of the committee of scientists that advised the administration said the group did not agree on new limits for the air pollutants, and needed more time and information.
But another scientist on the panel said while more time was needed, there was enough information on which to base tougher rules to protect public health from soot and smog.

"There was no consensus," George Wolff, chairman of the Environmental Protection Agency's Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee, said. He said it would take another five years to get adequate information.
Wolff, who is a scientist for General Motors Corp, chairs the panel made up of industry and academic experts.

Automobile manufacturers, along with other polluting industries, have argued against stricter standards, which they say will cost billions of dollars in pollution controls and produce minimal health benefits.

Morton Lippmann, of New York University's Insitute of Environmental Medicine and another committee member, said the EPA's proposed air quality standards fell within the ranges of recommendations of most of the panel members.
"What the administration proposed was a prudent step in the right direction," Lippmann said, adding that he would have preferred stricter new standards.
Republicans on the Senate panel, clearly sceptical of the administration's proposal, have said they wanted to see the medical and scientific justification for the new standards.

"These new standards for smog and soot are 25 percent to 35 percent more stringent than the current ones, and will require the expenditure of tens of billions of dollars," Rhode Island Republican John Chafee, who chairs the full Senate Environment Committee, said.
"We owe it to the American public to help search for the facts and truth behind the scientific claims," Oklahoma Republican James Inhofe, the subcommittee chairman, said.
Panel Democrats generally endorsed the proposal, saying it would protect the most vulnerable people including children, the elderly and people with asthma or emphysema.

"...we cannot allow the absence of absolute scientific certainty to paralyse us. As the saying goes, we can't let perfection become the enemy of the good," Sen. Max Baucus of Montana, the full committee's ranking Democrat, said.

Environmental groups meanwhile protested outside the hearing, saying the witness list for the subcommittee's hearing was stacked against the new standards, and that a number of the scientists who testified were on payrolls of polluting industries.
